prompt.context: It is early October, and Jimmy Smith, an MBA2 at NYU Stern, has a decision to make. After a summer interning at Firm A, Jimmy received an offer to return full-time next year. However, Jimmy also decided to re-recruit and received a competing offer from Firm B. Jimmy now needs to decide which offer he should accept, and has looked to you, his best friend, for help.
prompt.question: Which job offer should Jimmy accept — Firm A or Firm B? Help him make the best financial decision.

clarifying_info.q: What does Jimmy care about most?
clarifying_info.a: Jimmy only cares about money and is seeking to maximize financial value.

clarifying_info.q: Is Jimmy considering any other opportunities?
clarifying_info.a: No, Jimmy is not considering any other opportunities.

clarifying_info.q: How long does Jimmy plan to stay at the firm?
clarifying_info.a: Jimmy's intention is to work at either firm for 3 years.

clarifying_info.q: Are these firms in the same industry?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, Firms A and B are competitors in the same industry. Firm A is considered second-tier but increasingly competes with top-tier firms for talent. Firm B is more prestigious and is considered top-tier.

exhibits.title: Compensation Package by Firm
exhibits.shows: A table comparing the compensation components of Firm A and Firm B side by side

exhibits.title: Salary Growth by Firm (Years 1–3)
exhibits.shows: A chart showing projected annual salary growth for Firm A and Firm B over years 1 through 3; note states that annual bonus is expected to remain constant

exhibits.title: Distribution of Expected Starting Salaries for Exit Opportunities
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing the probability distribution of starting salaries at exit opportunities after 3 years, comparing top-tier (Firm B alumni) vs. second-tier (Firm A alumni) firms; note states salary will grow at 5% per year indefinitely

framework: Identify all sources of compensation: base salary, signing bonus, annual bonus, tuition reimbursement
Apply DCF/NPV methodology to discount all cash flows to present value (Year 0), since timing of cash flows matters
Compare 3-year NPV of Firm A vs. Firm B offer
Brainstorm additional financial and non-financial considerations beyond the 3-year window
Assess exit opportunities after Year 3 using expected value analysis and PV calculation
Synthesize all findings into a final recommendation

questions.prompt: Calculate the NPV of each firm's compensation package over 3 years using a discount rate implied by the simplified DCF rounding. Which firm has the higher 3-year NPV?
questions.guidance: Candidate must recognize that cash flows occur at different times (signing bonus at Year 0, salary+bonus each year, tuition reimbursement at Year 3). They should discount each year's total cash flow to present value. Firm A has slightly higher 3-year NPV ($440k vs $430k). The discount rate used is approximately 10% per year (simplified: Year 1 cash flows rounded to nearest $10k, e.g. $121k → $110k; Year 2 $144k → $120k; Year 3 $234k → $180k for Firm A).

math.setup: Total cash flows per year, then apply simplified discounting (round to nearest $10k). Discount factor: ~1.1^n approximation used in casebook.
steps: Firm A Totals: Year 0 = $30k (signing bonus), Year 1 = $91k + $30k = $121k, Year 2 = $114k + $30k = $144k, Year 3 = $126k + $30k + $78k = $234k
Firm A Simplified DCF: Year 0 = $30k, Year 1 ≈ $110k, Year 2 ≈ $120k, Year 3 ≈ $180k
Firm B Totals: Year 0 = $40k (signing bonus), Year 1 = $97k + $35k = $132k, Year 2 = $121k + $35k = $156k, Year 3 = $147k + $35k = $182k
Firm B Simplified DCF: Year 0 = $40k, Year 1 ≈ $120k, Year 2 ≈ $130k, Year 3 ≈ $140k
Conclusion: Firm A 3-year NPV ($440k) > Firm B 3-year NPV ($430k) by $10k
math.answer: Firm A has a higher 3-year NPV by approximately $10k ($440k vs $430k).

questions.prompt: After the 3-year NPV comparison, what other factors should Jimmy consider before making a final decision?
questions.guidance: Push for at least 4 ideas beyond initial framework. Financial: exit opportunities, firm financial security/stability. Non-financial: focus of firm's business, location, travel time, corporate culture, training quality, work type.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, calculate the expected value of exit opportunity salaries from each firm after 3 years. Then determine the present value of the salary differential to see if it changes the recommendation.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute weighted-average (expected value) of exit salaries, or use median with justification. Then calculate PV of the Year 4 salary differential using PV = FV / (1+r)^n. The $10k advantage of Firm A's 3-year NPV is overcome by Firm B's superior exit opportunities.

math.setup: Expected Value = sum of (Salary × Probability). Then PV = FV / (1 + r)^n using n=1 (year 4 is one period beyond year 3, r ≈ 40% cumulative discount or ~10% from year 3 perspective — casebook uses 1.4 as cumulative 3-year factor applied simply).
steps: Differential (median method): $225k − $175k = $50k (Firm A median ≈ $175k, Firm B median ≈ $225k)
Either way, PV of Firm B exit advantage ($25k–$35.7k) exceeds the $10k Firm A 3-year NPV lead
Note: 5% salary growth assumption is a red herring — it further widens Firm B's advantage but does not change the conclusion
math.answer: PV of Firm B exit salary advantage is ~$25k (mean) to ~$35.7k (median), which more than offsets Firm A's $10k higher 3-year NPV. Firm B is the better overall choice.

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond the quantitative financial comparison, what other things should Jimmy consider before accepting an offer?

categories.name: Financial
ideas: Exit opportunities and quality of alumni network
Firm financial health and job security
Likelihood of promotion and pay raises beyond stated projections
Benefits not captured in compensation table (healthcare, retirement contributions)

categories.name: Non-Financial
ideas: Prestige and brand-name value of each firm on resume
Focus of firm's business and type of work Jimmy would do
Quality of training and mentorship programs
Network and colleagues at each firm

recommendation: Although Firm A offers a marginally higher 3-year NPV ($440k vs $430k, a $10k difference), the present value of Firm B's superior exit opportunities ($25k–$36k advantage) more than compensates for this gap
The long-term career trajectory and earning potential from Firm B's top-tier exit opportunities decisively tilt the decision toward Firm B
risks: Firm B encounters financial challenges and lays off staff before Jimmy completes 3 years
Jimmy underperforms at Firm B and does not realize the benefits associated with its better exit opportunities
Firm B proves to be a poor cultural fit and Jimmy leaves before his three years are up
next_steps: Leverage Firm A offer as negotiating leverage to secure a better compensation package at Firm B
Conduct further due diligence on each firm, including cultural fit, type of work, and firm stability
Make the most of each firm's sell days and hold off on signing until the deadline to gather maximum information
